proportionality.description: Data Act applies different obligations based on role (data holder, user, data recipient, cloud provider, gatekeeper) and entity size. SME protections are built into several chapters.

tiers.name: data_holder_manufacturer
tiers.applies_to: Manufacturers and designers of connected products (IoT devices) and related services that generate data — Chapter II
tiers.note: Must make product data easily accessible to users by design (Art. 3). Must provide access upon request (Art. 4). Must make data available to third parties at user request (Art. 5). Fair, reasonable, non-discriminatory terms.

tiers.name: data_recipient
tiers.applies_to: Third parties receiving data at user request — Chapter II
tiers.note: Must not use data to develop competing connected product (Art. 6(2)(e)). Must not share with gatekeepers (Art. 6(2)(d)). Subject to FRAND terms. Must delete data when no longer needed.

tiers.name: b2b_data_sharing
tiers.applies_to: Any contractual data sharing between businesses — Chapter III
tiers.note: Unfair contract terms in data access contracts are not binding (Art. 13). Compensation must be reasonable. SME protections: compensation for data made available to SMEs must not exceed costs (Art. 9(4)).

tiers.name: b2g_data_sharing
tiers.applies_to: Public sector access to private data in cases of exceptional need — Chapter V
tiers.note: Only for exceptional need: public emergencies, statutory tasks where data not otherwise obtainable. Proportionate requests. Compensation (marginal cost for SMEs, reasonable for others). Data must be destroyed when no longer needed.

tiers.name: cloud_switching
tiers.applies_to: Cloud service providers and data processing service providers — Chapter VI
tiers.note: Customer right to switch providers or port data. Switching charges must be reduced to zero by 2027-01-12. Functional equivalence obligations for IaaS. Provider must assist with porting, remove switching barriers.

tiers.name: gatekeeper_restrictions
tiers.note: Third-party data recipients must NOT make data available to gatekeepers. Gatekeepers must not request, incentivise, or coerce users to share IoT data obtained under the Data Act. This prevents data concentration.

derogations.description: Data holder may refuse data access request if disclosure would undermine trade secret protection. But must demonstrate specific risk and propose protective measures (Art. 4(6)). Blanket refusal not permitted.

derogations.applies_to: Micro and small enterprises as data holders
derogations.description: Chapter II (data access) and Chapter III (B2B terms) do NOT apply to micro/small enterprises as manufacturers/data holders. They benefit from SME protections as data recipients.
Data Act does not affect GDPR. Where IoT data includes personal data, both apply. Data Act access rights do not override GDPR legal bases.

pitfalls.description: Art. 3 is a DESIGN obligation, not just an access obligation. Connected products and related services must be designed and manufactured so that data generated by their use is, by default, easily, securely, and directly accessible to the user. This applies from product design stage — retrofitting access to existing products is harder. Products placed on market after Sep 2025 must comply.

IoT data is often a mix of personal and non-personal data. Where personal data is included, GDPR applies in full alongside the Data Act. The user requesting access under Art. 4 may not be the data subject. Where data cannot be separated, the entire dataset must be treated as personal data. This creates complex dual-regulation compliance.

Data recipients must NOT make IoT data available to gatekeepers (as designated under DMA). This is an absolute prohibition, not a balancing test. Violating this risks both Data Act penalties and DMA implications. Practical impact: business models involving sharing IoT data with designated gatekeepers (Google, Apple, Meta, Amazon, Microsoft, ByteDance) are prohibited.

Cloud switching charges must be reduced to zero by 12 January 2027 (3 years after entry into force). During the transition period, charges must be progressively reduced. After the deadline, providers may only charge direct costs of the switching process itself. Provider-imposed minimum contract periods are capped at 12 months.

Trade secret protection is not a blanket exemption from data access. Data holder must identify the specific data and the specific risk, and must propose proportionate technical and organisational measures to preserve trade secret confidentiality (confidentiality agreements, access controls). Only if measures are insufficient may access be refused — and the user may challenge before a competent body.

Art. 36 introduces requirements for smart contracts used for data sharing: safe termination mechanism, archiving capability, access control, right to continue to be consistent. This applies to automated data sharing agreements executed via smart contracts on distributed ledgers.

cross_regulation.note: Data Act explicitly does not affect GDPR. Where IoT data includes personal data, both apply simultaneously. Data Act access rights do not create a new GDPR legal basis. GDPR data subject rights (erasure, portability) apply independently.

Data Act prohibits sharing IoT data with DMA-designated gatekeepers. DMA gatekeeper designation (Art. 3) determines the scope of Data Act Art. 6(2)(d). The regulations reinforce each other against data concentration.

Data Governance Act creates governance framework for data intermediaries and data altruism. Data Act provides substantive access rights. DGA-recognised intermediaries may facilitate Data Act data sharing.

IoT products subject to Data Act data access requirements are also subject to CRA cybersecurity requirements. Data access mechanisms designed under Data Act Art. 3 must meet CRA Annex I security requirements.
Financial Data Access Regulation (proposed) creates sector-specific data sharing rules for financial services. Where FIDA applies, it is lex specialis to the Data Act for financial data.

key_structures.title: Design obligation — data accessibility by default
key_structures.description: Para 1: products must be designed so generated data is accessible to the user easily, securely, free of charge, and where technically feasible in real-time. Para 2: users must be informed before purchase about what data is generated, how to access it, whether manufacturer intends to use it, and for what purpose. Para 3: data must be made available in a structured, commonly used, machine-readable format.

key_structures.title: User right to access data — the core access right
key_structures.description: Para 1: user may request and receive data generated by use of connected product or related service. Para 2: data holder must make data available without undue delay, free of charge, continuously, in real-time where feasible. Para 3-5: data must be comprehensive, structured, machine-readable, of same quality as available to data holder. Para 6: trade secret protection — specific measures, not blanket refusal.

key_structures.title: Cloud switching — right to switch and port
key_structures.description: Para 1: cloud/data processing providers must not impose barriers to switching. Para 2: must enable data export in structured, commonly used format. Para 3: switching period maximum 30 calendar days. Para 4: functional equivalence obligations for IaaS. Art. 29: switching charges reduced to zero by Jan 2027.

key_recitals.clarifies: Connected product scope — physical items that obtain, generate, or collect data by means of components or operating systems and can communicate that data. Includes IoT, industrial machinery, consumer electronics with connectivity.
User definition — natural or legal person that owns, rents, or leases a connected product, or receives a related service. Both consumers and businesses qualify as users.
Cloud switching rationale — vendor lock-in through switching barriers inhibits competition and digital sovereignty. Zero switching charges after transition period ensure effective portability.

Gatekeeper restriction rationale — preventing gatekeepers from accumulating IoT data that strengthens their market position. The restriction applies regardless of whether the user consents to the sharing.

national_implementation.pattern: Data Act is a regulation (directly applicable). Member States designate competent authorities (Art. 37). No national transposition needed but enforcement structures vary.

evidence_hint: Call get_evidence_requirements(regulation='DATA_ACT') for per-article audit artifacts. Key artifacts: Product data access design documentation (Art. 3), User information provided before purchase (Art. 3(2)), Data sharing contracts/terms (Art. 8-9), Trade secret protection measures (Art. 4(6)), Cloud switching capability documentation (Art. 23-31), Smart contract compliance documentation (Art. 36).

timeline.note: Published in Official Journal. 20-month implementation period.

timeline.event: Full application — all Data Act requirements
timeline.note: All obligations applicable. Products placed on market from this date must comply with Art. 3 design obligation.

timeline.event: Chapter VI cloud switching charges must be zero
timeline.note: Art. 29: all cloud switching and data porting charges must be reduced to zero (3 years after entry into force).

citation_format: Cite as: Data Act Art. X(Y). Note: Data Act is Regulation (EU) 2023/2854.
